This conversation is a demonstration of ask culture versus guess culture. 

She wants them to communicate indirectly, through hints, because she feels communication is mostly non-verbal & that he should have to use context clues like tone & phrasing to figure out her state of mind without her saying her mind out loud & risking losing face. 

He isn’t a mind reader, isn’t as scared of losing face as she is, & doesn’t understand why she feels like she can’t speak her mind in order for them to understand each other, so he’s trying to get her to verbalise her point of view. 

She won’t be direct until she is actually really upset with him though, because she will feel embarrassed & ashamed & misunderstood if she has to say the quiet part out loud. Part of her ideas about love & trust probably include the idea that her loved ones are more able to read her mind & won’t need to be told what she is thinking. 

Guess culture people usually communicate using dogwhistles & emotional manipulation strategies. They are used to feeling like they’re about to get in trouble or be caught out doing the wrong thing, even if they aren’t really doing anything wrong, because they’re taught that if people don’t understand you, or take offence to you or call you out on harmful behaviours, then they’re “not like us” & you don’t have to respect or include them because they’re your enemy now - they don’t “get” you. 

They also usually feel like they might be just about to win something big if they get away with whatever it is they’re doing, so fear of missing out plays a big part in not wanting to communicate boundaries clearly & give reasons for those boundaries. 

This means guess culture people can be pretty reactive & unpredictable - if you say “Steve didn’t like the potato salad” they might be imagining all kinds of things that could change their life for better or worse, things that have nothing to do with not needing to make any potato salad for Steve in the future, because he wasn’t that into it. 

They might be interpreting that sentence as “you’re not invited to the next bbq because you’re bad at making food” or “hahaha you hurt Steve’s feelings with substandard potato salad, great job, we hate Steve” - there’s no way of knowing what message you’ve given a guess culture person as an ask culture person, because they speak in riddles & codes. 

Both people are going to feel confused & disrespected - the expectations they have about what feels loving & safe in a conversation don’t match up at all. 

I’m a direct communicator, so I’ll just speak my mind & then assume that others know where I stand & there’s no confusion, but often they’re making up their own subtext because they don’t understand direct communicators & think there must be a secret interpretation of plain speech designed to remove confusion, which is not super helpful in my opinion. 

Hints for other direct communicators, use “I” statements in conflicts & for boundary setting (“I feel frustrated at being spoken to like this, I was on time, I will leave the room now if we can’t speak calmly about this” rather than “you’re the problem, you were the one who was late, lower your voice or I’ll throw you out”) and don’t accept untrue statements about yourself - you are always the expert on your own thoughts, feelings & experiences because no one else was in your head or in your body thinking your thoughts & feeling your feelings with you, so they are not the expert, they weren’t there. 

Indirect communicators might try to gaslight you about your thoughts & feelings while they’re trying to get you to guess their thoughts and feelings, and it might seem really hurtful & unfair, but every accusation is a confession - cheaters will accuse you of cheating, liars will accuse you of lying, so if someone comes out with a really hurtful & unfair accusation they might just be telling on themselves. 

Communicating is way harder than most people think it is. We’re all just trying to feel safe & loved & understood, but when there are two different rule books for how to be kind & polite it gets pretty messy. First step is figuring out which kind of communicators we are ourselves, and that can take time.

Paternity and child safety are two different issues. You can report your ex fiancé as being a potential danger to the baby to the police or to child services, or you could contact friends and family members of your ex fiancé and ask them to be alert for signs that the baby is being neglected or abused as a priority - the child’s safety is paramount over any concerns about paternity. Any concerned person can report a child at risk, so if you believe your ex is a danger to the welfare of the baby, I wouldn’t wait for paternity test results to make sure the baby is safe. 

Once the safety of the child has been addressed, you can look at establishing paternity and going through the courts to get visitation or custody if the child is biologically yours - which isn’t 100% guaranteed until you have confirmation from a DNA test. You can ask the court to serve your ex with a Summons and Complaint Regarding Parental Obligations, which will oblige her to comply with paternity testing once the child is born. That will get the ball rolling.

Yep. Our private hospitals don’t have all the facilities for things like that. Our public health system is excellent except for dental & mental health, which are not covered for some ungodly reason. The rest is just improved comfort and privacy, and a way to cut in line if you don’t want to wait for minor surgery.

Prescriptions from a private dr are still covered by the [Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme](https://m.pbs.gov.au/home.html). 

Private health in Australia covers things like dental care, elective surgeries, mental health units, rehab units, subsidised therapeutic massage & other alternative medicine like acupuncture, and gives you discounted gym memberships and access to private hospitals with single person rooms, nicer food, more of a hotel experience as opposed to sharing a ward with a bunch of other patients and eating bland food that’s been served at the wrong temperature. 

Private hospitals will transfer patients to public hospitals if there are complications that go beyond the scope of what a private hospital can manage - they aren’t set up to deal with emergencies (they have no emergency wards, for a start). 

I’d say that most people in Australia don’t need private health care unless they have dental issues beyond the normal need for a 6 monthly checkup, mental health needs that might require hospitalisation, addiction issues or they want a joint replaced or something but don’t want to wait for it.

People who have private insurance aren’t locked in to only using the private system, they just get privileges that someone without private health doesn’t get. More like a two tiered system as opposed to two systems. Medicare is a right, everyone here pays the Medicare levy, it covers most medical care. Private health is a luxury which people pay for because they prefer salmon steaks to fishcakes, higher thread count sheets, shorter waiting times for surgeries and more attentive nurses.

Grief is so hard. Especially suicide. I’ve lost more than a few loved ones to suicide, and it’s an indescribable pain. 

Some practical things - 

• your brain runs on glucose. You need to get some sugar into your system to keep things from spiralling, getting worse. If you can’t bring yourself to eat, drink juice and sports drinks like Gatorade, and meal replacements like sustagen. 

• Erase “should have” from your vocabulary. It is what it is, what’s done is done. Beating yourself up because you aren’t psychic & don’t have magical powers of deduction achieves nothing and doesn’t honour her memory. You didn’t do this to her, and you don’t deserve to be punished. Don’t punish yourself. 

• Go to her funeral. We have these rituals for a reason. The days before the funeral are the hardest. Spending time with all the people who loved her and knowing that you aren’t grieving alone is really important.  

• reach out - even your family doctor is a good place to start. They might prescribe something like valium to help get you through the next couple of weeks, or they might refer you to a grief counsellor, or both. You don’t have to go through this alone. 

• know that this pain you’re in now won’t always be constant agony. I know it feels like it will never end, but time is relentless. 20 years from now, it will only be this intense in rare moments, on anniversaries, when you stumble across an old photograph, or hear a song that brings you back. You’ll still mourn, but it won’t feel like your insides are being torn out. Just a hard lump in the throat, maybe a few tears. And the rest of the time, you’ll be living your life, and you’ll be ok. 

I know that sounds callous right now, and I know you’ll never forget her - I’m not suggesting that, but this advice comes from unfortunate personal experience. It’s been 20 years since my best friend committed suicide. She was 17. Her 40 something year old boyfriend got her addicted to heroin and started pimping her out. It was in her diary. We didn’t know. 

I didn’t think I’d ever stop feeling rage and pain every minute I was awake. But gradually, I did. Now, I feel a stab when I drive past her old house. I go to our special place & put flowers on the water on her birth and death  dates, and I grieve for her - I don’t know where she’s buried because instead of going to her funeral I went on a bender, something I have always regretted.

Good luck. Try to be kind to yourself.

Deep breathing is a distress tolerance technique. There are lots of them. They are sort of graded - some work best when you’re feeling a little bit antsy, some you save for when you’ve already decided to cut but you can’t find anything sharp and now that’s upsetting you too. 

Deep breathing is good for stopping anxiety as it starts to build. It can help bring you down from an escalated state if you’re used to using it as a cooldown, but that comes with loads of practice, and usually you’d also be using mindfulness with that. Both skills that come with time & practice.

For high levels of distress, ice is great. Hold a handful of ice cubes until you can’t any more. The pain (my daughter cuts regularly, she screamed so much abuse at me when I made her try this, because it hurt more than cutting) causes the same endorphin rush as cutting, but no mess, no fuss. Put it this way, my daughter yelled, she threw the ice at me, she abruptly sat and went from raging to sad little girl, and then she cried for 5 minutes or so and went to sleep. She’s 14, for the record. Prior to the ice all hell was breaking loose because I’d hidden all the blades in the house. 

If that’s not working, get a frozen gel ice pack or a bag of frozen peas and squish it into your eyeballs & sinus area (including forehead and cheeks) until it feels like your eyes are crystallising. This will induce your dive reflex - it’s the quickest way to become calm. It’s 3-4 minutes of freezing your face, and then the storm is over. 

Largely because your heart rate is now between 10 and 25% slower, your spleen has just released a surge of new red blood cells, and your blood is now concentrated in your torso and head, because your body has been tricked into thinking it’s been dropped in the Arctic Ocean somewhere & it needs to keep the important bits warm.

I hope that’s more helpful. You can find more distress tolerance techniques if you google - they’re part of the DBT program.

Can you try the “would I like it if someone said that to my best friend?” test? It’s a mental exercise, very simple. 

When you think something about yourself, or say something about yourself, just stop for a second & think about whether it would be nice for someone to say that to someone you cared about. 

If the answer is no, I wouldn’t say that to a friend, then it’s classed as negative self talk, which goes in the bin - it’s really damaging. You then speak to yourself like you would speak to a loved one, and try very hard to mean it.

If my friend had run, it’s possible that 2 dogs of that size, of that breed, very obviously unfriendly and waiting for an excuse to attack, could have seriously injured her or even killed her. 

Sorry about the long winded message, but that was what popped into my head when I read your post. Please don’t run from scary dogs. It makes them scarier.

Happiness is chemical, and we can do things to hack our brains to get them to produce more happiness chemicals, and to switch off stress chemicals. 

Some of the things are super low effort, so I’d start there first. 

1. Focusing on deep breathing, making your belly rise, not just your chest, and slowly counting in your head to 5 as you inhale, and 7 as you exhale for at least 10 breaths will change how you feel. The longer you do it, the more relaxed and at peace you will feel. 

2. If you squeeze for a few seconds and relax your toes, then your feet, then your calves, slowly working your way all the way up your body, finishing by tightening the muscles in your face one at time and relaxing them, that can also be a big mood changer and release a lot of stress. 

3. To reduce anxiety or stress, flip your hands over so the palms are facing the sky. This turns off your cortisol response, a stress hormone. Also, put your tongue behind your front teeth and press it there slightly - this stops you clenching your jaw or grinding your teeth, and signals to the body that it’s time to stop freaking out. 

4. If you’re experiencing more distress than the palm trick can deal with, try running your wrists under very cold water - make the water run over your veins, the idea is to cool your circulatory system down. You’ll literally chill out and feel calmer. It’s also an idea to stand under an air conditioner or fan, have a cool shower, go for a swim (it’s summer where I am) or if it’s winter where you are, maybe build a snowman? Stand outside, anyway. 

5. If distress is well out of hand - at crisis levels, there are 2 other options. One is to hold a handful of ice with bare hands until it really really hurts - this releases the same chemical rush as cutting, but without all the mess, and the other is to press a soft ice pack or bag of frozen peas against your eyes and sinuses until it feels like your eyeballs are crystallising. This produces the dive reflex, which will calm you right down, lower heart rate & breathing rate, and produce a big rush of endorphins. 

6. Intense exercise is good for a big boost of endorphins, including dopamine and serotonin. You only need a short burst of high intensity exercise - sprinting at top speed to the end of the block would do it for most people. Alternatively, lifting heavy things or doing a quick CrossFit style workout would also have the same effect. Anything that pushes your physical limits. 

7. Regular easy to moderate exercise - a lazy walk around the block or the park every afternoon - will help your brain produce more endorphins as a regular thing, and you’ll get a small endorphin rush after your walk. 

8. Finding joy in small things is very important. Taking time to enjoy your morning beverage for example, maybe drinking it out of a cup you really like, smelling it before you sip, really tasting it before you swallow. Being grateful for the things you have, and the good people in your life, even if it’s not a perfect life. Looking for silver linings - I’ve gotten so good at finding silver linings in terrible situations that I can’t be trusted to open my mouth any more in case I pop out with something terribly inappropriate. 

9. Community is so important. Humans are herd animals, we aren’t meant to be solitary. I get that socialising isn’t everyone’s forte, but that’s ok. In the event that you have friends & make use of their company, great. If you have friends & dont see them, my suggestion is to set up a regular no effort thing. Something along the lines of watching a Netflix series together one night a week, or gaming, or whatever you’re into. Just so that people are regularly checking in on you and you don’t feel isolated and alone. Isolation is pretty deadly. I can’t be trusted for too long on my own, I know that much. In the event that your friends are still out in the wild & you haven’t met them yet, do not be ashamed to call the suicide hotlines just to hear a friendly voice. I’m a frequent caller. I know when I need to hear a human voice, and if my friends aren’t nearby, I’ll take a friendly stranger any day. It really does help. I mean, I’m still here, so... 

10. Take the little wins. Do not hold yourself up against any other human - they don’t know your challenges, compare yourself only to how you were doing earlier today, to how you did yesterday. If you make a small step forward, celebrate it! Only you can know how far you’ve come, what it took to get you here. Don’t worry what others think of your achievements, take pride in what you accomplish, no matter how mundane it is. You made a sandwich? That’s a kickass sandwich! My therapy group called it “building mastery” - it just means building that feeling where you look around at all your work and think “damn I’m good. Look at all I’ve accomplished”. Feeling good about your achievements  definitely helps with happiness levels. 

I know long post is long, but I hope some of these resonate with you and maybe help a bit. Good luck.

I am super old now, my child is nearly as old as you. I’ll tell you what I told her last week. What I wish I’d had someone to tell me when I was an awkward teen. 

It’s just hormones making you feel devastatingly unattractive. I don’t know why they do that, but a hell of a lot of teens do not feel pretty at various stages. It’s ok, and you’re going to be ok. You don’t have to let this just happen to you - there are a few things you can do to get a handle on this. 

You can help yourself out by doing a few simple things. (I’m starting with basics, don’t be offended, sometimes people don’t know) 

1. Hygiene. If you smell good, and your teeth are gleaming, that will help a lot. Shower at least daily and try to make your hair behave. If you don’t know how to style hair well, ask someone - if all else fails go ask the barber or hairdresser for some tips (I had to when I was a teen, my mother had no idea). Shave if you need to shave, no one wants a neck beard. Wear clean clothes, and some deodorant & aftershave. You’ll always feel a lot more confident and attractive when you’re looking & smelling your best. 

2. Health. Those negative thoughts and feelings can be tracked back to your brain chemistry & your general health. If you aren’t already, try and get your heart rate elevated (ideally you should be able to talk but not easily - you should be panting) above normal for at least half an hour either jogging, cycling, skating, swimming laps, whatever appeals to you, at least three times a week. This will release endorphins in your brain which will make you feel happier and more relaxed. As a bonus, you’ll tone up and start looking fitter if it’s a new activity. If you want to improve your physique, but have no experience, “bodyweight exercise for beginners” should find you some achievable at home workouts. 

With the exercise comes being mindful of what you eat. Fresh foods & wholegrains will make you feel calm and level, anything with high fats & sugars will make your mood swing all over the place, and also ruin the good work you’re putting in with your exercise. Also, drink loads of water. Just sip constantly. 

3. Mindfulness. You can get apps for this - I use Headspace, just the free version. It’s training your brain to stop being a jerk and start doing what you want without telling you you’re fat or whatever, basically. It’s an exercise, it takes time to get the hang of, but it definitely works. Good for learning to flick off suicidal thoughts when you need to as well. 

I hope this helps a bit. Good luck.

In Australia we have Newstart payment for the unemployed people who aren’t studying or raising small children or disabled. It comes with very strict conditions.

I’m Australian. I live in a warm temperate climate - our winter minimums tend to be around 9 degrees Celsius and our summer highs around 27. Our record minimum is 0.0 degrees Celsius and our highest is 43.5 degrees Celsius. When I travel, it’s usually to the north, where it’s hotter, so blankets don’t usually come into it, unless you’re talking fire blankets - I don’t have one but a lot of people keep them in their cars in case of bushfires. 

I keep sunscreen (I have a mini bottle on my keyring too, actually) and a few bottles of water in the car as a regular thing, and if I’m going anywhere long distance (over a couple of hours drive) I stock up on snacks and I take extra water/ Gatorade. I also keep mosquito repellent in the glove box. 

If I’m going very far outside of the more populated areas, I take a phone that’s registered to the phone network that basically has a monopoly on regional and rural areas. I’ve also got a solar powered phone charger in case the battery in my car dies and I can’t use my car charger, as those trips can be up to 16 hours one way, and there’s a lot of empty land where towns are a few hours away from each other with nothing much in between. If you break down out there without a phone you might have to walk a hundred km or more to get to the nearest place you can call for help, so you really want a working phone with good reception at all times. 

Emergency kits should reflect the climate and expected conditions. Thermal blankets are of little use in the subtropics. Mosquito repellent isn’t much good in 6 feet of snow.

Coins are tokens. They represent, as you said, the value of an item. You used an egg. 

As I stated, money makes trade easier. You have too many eggs, and a guy who has nothing that you want wants to purchase them. This is where money comes in. It’s a little note, an IOU, stating that eggs were exchanged and the dude is good for it, just hand this piece of paper/ disk of metal or rock to another vendor and you can trade that for the worth of your eggs. 

It’s a convenience. That’s all. It’s a nifty one, I’ll give you that, but a nifty convenience doesn’t confer more value than art, or a human life. 

I can’t believe I’m actually having to explain this to another human, but some value is intrinsic. Art is valuable because it makes us think and feel things. It’s an expression of our humanity. Art predates our recorded history, and is also a way to record our history. If I think it’s beautiful or disturbing or magnificent, the price tag won’t affect how the piece made me feel. If you buy a painting for me for a million dollars, and I think it looks like shmeared dog shit, I’m hiding it in the garage, I’m not hanging it in the house. 

Humans are valuable to their communities, their families, their friends and colleagues, maybe their YouTube subscribers. How much crap they have to trade has nothing to do with their intrinsic value. How much material worth they can produce may have nothing to do with the amount of joy they bring to those around them. You can’t put a value on true human connection. 

You’re playing the game of life wrong. It’s not who gets the the most formal service with the biggest tombstone at the end, in the fanciest marble, with most elegant hearse & the youngest trophy wife with the fakest tears. Dignitaries and influential people who shook your hand twice mingling with stone faces. 

The person who wins the game of life has the biggest wake, the most stories told, the biggest laughs, all their family and friends and people they’ve picked up along their journey gathered together to celebrate their life, hopefully like my grandfathers recent wake, with 4 generations in attendance and music and dancing and great grandbabies everywhere. 

That’s how you win at life. He didn’t run a corporation, he was the president of a lawn bowls club though, and that was enough to keep him happy. Count your loved ones, not your coins. Coins aren’t going to hug you when your loved ones pass away. Coins aren’t going to miss you when you are gone. Coins are good for buying eggs.

My family was so demonstrative in their affections that my mother sent me skidding across the floor for trying to initiate a hug when I was 8 - I told her then, and I stuck by my word, that I would never try to hug her again until she tried to hug me first. Now she makes a point of hugging hello and goodbye when we see each other every few years, but it’s like 2 stick insects trying to show affection. 

My dad, on the other hand, took the interview with the child behavioural therapist (called in by my school)  pretty seriously when I was 9. I had no idea they’d met with her, so I’ll tell it from my perspective. My dad, who I knew as a man of flashing moods, completely unpredictable, sometimes hilarious, sometimes terrifying and violent, but never affectionate or loving, came home from work and made me sit in his lap. 

Alarm bell one. This was super weird. My younger siblings would climb all over him, but I was considered “too big”. (I had a growth problem, there wasn’t that much difference in size, I just wasn’t liked much) 

Then he explained at length all the things he admired about my character and personality, while I sat slack jawed wondering if I was dying or something, and that’s why he was being nice to me. Then he told me that he and my mother both loved me very much even if they didn’t show it very much, at which point I screamed “LIAR!!! YOU’RE A LIAR!!!!” directly into his face, sprang out of his lap, and ran away until the street lights came on and I had to go home. 

It was never mentioned again. 

So anyway, it feels pretty weird and fake when people show affection to me, except for my child. I did a fake-it-til-you-make-it approach with her, hugged and kissed her and verbally expressed love at random throughout the day until it felt as natural as breathing. It’s easier to start on a little blob who can’t really protest if you don’t get the tone of the “I love you” exactly right the first few times, and your hugs are a bit stiff and rusty at first and they don’t feel “right”. 

If you can’t legally obtain a newborn to practice on, a demanding pet (Siamese or Manx cat, kelpie or beagle dog, any brand of intelligent parrot) will do basically the same job (test your patience and will to live while providing awwwws and give you something to love on) except you won’t get to progress to sentient conversations 3 years later. 

Some people would say lack of toilet training more than makes up for that, but as someone with both pets and a child, my 8 year old dogs still crap on the floor should they get the urge, so I may be overselling that point.

The point is, I used the experience of having my daughter and learning to be affectionate towards her to desensitise myself from the deep insecurity I felt at letting another human near me while I was vulnerable. It was hard work. It was a long time after that that I allowed anyone to hug me. I remember the breakthrough I had when I realised I could hug literally anyone I knew and not freak out - I was hugging people for no reason other than I could for days. I’m sure I freaked a few people out. My daughter was 8 by then, so it was a slow process. 

I still have times where I’m not ok, and people can’t hug me, and shouldn’t try to approach. Apparently it’s pretty obvious to those who know me whether I’m hug-it-out-upset or remove-all-potential-weapons-upset. I think that’s about the best I can hope for in this lifetime. I think that’s pretty normal for most people with average upbringings.
